readerTitle: When Nespresso's capsule patents ran out
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Nestlé의 Nespresso, 특허 만료와 호환 캡슐 경쟁) + 가상 적용 (스마트 온도조절기와 앱 구독)
insight: 면도기·면도날 모델의 이익은 소모품 자체가 아니라 다른 회사가 그 소모품을 팔지 못하게 막는 울타리에서 나온다. 그 울타리에는 만료일이 있으므로, 만료 전에 다음 울타리를 세워야 한다.
misconception: 기계를 많이 깔아 두면 캡슐 이익은 저절로 계속 들어온다. 소모품 이익은 기계가 지켜 준다.

sources.text: Nestlé Nespresso, company history (1986 launch, Nespresso Club, first boutique in Paris)
Press coverage of key Nespresso capsule patents expiring around 2012 and compatible capsules entering supermarkets (e.g., Reuters, Financial Times)
Autorité de la concurrence (France), 2014 decision accepting commitments from Nespresso on machine changes and rival capsules
Nespresso press materials on the launch of the VertuoLine system in North America (2014)
Nestlé annual reports (Nespresso described as one of the group's major businesses)

factChecks.note: 1986년 출시, 초기 사무실·업소 시장 부진 후 가정용으로 전환, 1989년 Nespresso Club 시작은 Nespresso 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요.
주요 캡슐 특허 만료 시점을 '2012년경'으로 적었습니다. 특허별로 만료 시점이 다르므로 원문 보도를 확인하고 문구를 '약'으로 유지하세요.
'여러 나라의 법원이 호환 캡슐을 막지 못했다'는 Ethical Coffee Company, Denner 등 소송 결과를 요약한 표현입니다. 일부 소송은 결과가 엇갈렸으므로 게시 전 확인하세요.
프랑스 경쟁당국의 2014년 결정(Nespresso의 시정 약속 수용) 번호와 내용(기계 변경 사전 고지, 보증 관련)을 확인하세요.
기계를 Krups, De'Longhi 등 파트너 가전업체가 만들고 판매한다는 점, 기계를 손해 보고 팔지 않는다는 일반적 설명을 확인하세요. 카드에는 '원가 이하'라는 표현을 쓰지 않았습니다.
첫 부티크(파리, 2000년), George Clooney 광고(2006년경 시작), Vertuo(2014년 북미 출시, 바코드 인식 캡슐) 연도를 확인하세요.
결과 카드의 매출·점유율은 수치 없이 정성적으로만 적었습니다(호환 캡슐이 상당한 점유율 확보, Nespresso는 Nestlé의 주요 사업으로 유지). 구체적 수치를 넣으려면 Nestlé 연차보고서로 확인하세요.

cards.title: When Nespresso's capsule patents ran out
body: Nestlé launched Nespresso in 1986. Partner appliance brands built and sold the machines. Nestlé sold the capsules, and for years only its own capsules fit.
That looked like a perfect razors-and-blades business: sell the machine once, sell the coffee every morning.
Then, around 2012, key capsule patents began to expire. Rivals were ready with cheaper capsules that fit the same machines.

image.label: A single espresso capsule beside a home coffee machine
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주방 조리대 위 캡슐 커피머신 한 대와 캡슐 하나. 캡슐 옆에 작은 자물쇠가 막 풀리는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고, 캡슐 색상 디자인, 기계 형태는 특정 제품과 닮지 않게.

cards.title: Copies are coming to the supermarket.
body: You run Nespresso. Millions of homes own your machines. Soon, any company can sell capsules that fit them, and supermarkets will stock them at lower prices.
What is your main response?

options.text: Cut capsule prices to match the supermarket copies
options.feedback: You may keep more customers, but you give up the margin that pays for the whole business. You also teach buyers that your capsule is just another capsule.

options.text: Fight hard: sue the rivals and change the machines so copies don't fit
options.feedback: This can buy time. But courts may not agree, regulators may step in, and customers who already own the machine may resent being blocked.

options.text: Give people reasons to buy from you that a patent never provided
options.feedback: Slower and costly, but it doesn't expire on a set date. It also doesn't stop copies from taking some share.

cards.title: Nespresso tried the fight first.
body: Compatible capsules arrived from several companies, sold in ordinary shops. Nespresso took rivals to court in several countries. Courts largely did not stop them.
Some machine design changes also drew attention. In 2014, France's competition authority accepted commitments from Nespresso about how it changed machines in ways that affected rival capsules.
The legal fence around the capsules was mostly gone. Whatever kept customers buying Nespresso's own capsules would have to come from somewhere else.

cards.title: The profit is in the fence, not the blade.
body: In a razors-and-blades model, you earn over time from the refill. But a refill is easy to copy. What really protects the profit is **the fence**: whatever stops others from selling refills for your machine.

Fences come in kinds. Some expire, like patents. Some can be challenged, like technical locks. Some have to be earned again every year, like brand, service and a direct relationship with the customer.

image.label: A capsule inside a fence with gates labelled patent, lock and brand
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 캡슐 하나를 울타리가 둘러쌈. 울타리 판자마다 라벨: "Patent (expires)", "Technical lock (can be challenged)", "Brand and relationship (earned every year)". 특허 판자에는 모래시계 아이콘. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: What Nespresso had built alongside the patents
body: Long before 2012, Nespresso had been building fences that patents didn't create:
list: **A direct relationship:** the Nespresso Club, started in 1989, sold capsules straight to members
**Its own shops:** boutiques, starting in Paris in 2000
**A premium brand:** years of high-profile ads, including with George Clooney
**Services:** capsule recycling programs and easy reordering
**A new system:** Vertuo, launched in North America in 2014, with capsules the machine reads by barcode
cards.callout: Copies could match the shape of a capsule. They couldn't copy the experience around buying it.

cards.title: The copies took share. The business survived.
body: Compatible capsules won a large slice of the capsule market, mostly with lower prices. The old near-monopoly on refills did not come back.
Yet Nespresso stayed one of Nestlé's major businesses, and many customers kept paying more for its own capsules. What held them wasn't a law. It was habit, convenience, shops and brand.
The counterexample: the machine alone never guaranteed the refill profit. The fences did, and the most durable ones were the ones built by hand.

cards.title: Every fence has a price.
body: Brand and service fences cost money every year: shops, ads, staff, recycling. They only pay off if customers value them enough to pay the premium.
New patents, like a new capsule system, restart the clock. They protect you for a while and then the same question returns.
And blocking rivals through the machine itself can backfire. It invites regulators and tells customers that the product they bought works against them.

cards.title: Now it's a smart thermostat.
body: You sell a smart thermostat at a thin margin. You make your money from a monthly app subscription that shows energy savings.
A new open standard will soon let any app connect to your thermostat. Rival apps will be cheaper. What do you do?

options.text: Update the firmware so only your app can connect
options.feedback: It protects the subscription for now, but it fights a standard customers expect. You risk angry reviews, returns and regulator attention.

options.text: Halve the subscription price to stay cheaper than rivals
options.feedback: It may slow switching, but it shrinks the very income the thin thermostat margin depends on. Price alone is a fence anyone can climb.

options.text: Make the app clearly better: smarter savings, easy setup, real support
options.feedback: This builds a fence the standard can't open. It costs ongoing effort, and some price-sensitive users will still leave.

cards.title: Know what fence protects your refill, and when it ends.
body: A refill business is only as strong as whatever stops others from selling the refill. Patents and locks expire or get challenged. Relationships and service have to be earned, but they last.
**Try it today:** name the repeat purchase your business depends on. Write down what stops a rival from selling it, and when that protection could end.
